source_text: Ἐκ δὲ τούτου αὐτοῖς ὑπάρχει ἀρνεῖσθαι μὲν τὸν μέγαν Θεὸν τῆς συστάσεως τῶν ὄντων προεστηκέναι, οἷον δὲ ἐράνου τινὸς πληρωτὴν, ὀλίγην τινὰ μοῖραν εἰς τὴν τῶν ὄντων γένεσιν παρ' ἑαυτοῦ συμβεβλῆσθαι· οὐ δυνη θέντες διὰ λογισμῶν ταπεινότητα πρὸς τὸ ὕψος ἀπιδεῖν τῆς ἀληθείας· ὅτι ἐνταῦθα μὲν αἱ τέχναι τῶν ὑλῶν ὕστεραι, διὰ τὸ ἀναγκαῖον τῆς χρείας παρεισαχθεῖσαι τῷ βίῳ. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἔριον προϋπῆρχεν, ἡ δὲ ὑφαντικὴ ἐπεγένετο, τὸ τῆς φύσεως ἐνδέον παρ' ἑαυτῆς ἐκπληροῦσα. Καὶ τὸ μὲν ξύλον ἦν, τεκτονικὴ δὲ παραλαβοῦσα, πρὸς τὴν ἐπιζητουμένην ἑκάστοτε χρείαν διαμορφοῦσα τὴν ὕλην, τὴν εὐχρηστίαν ἡμῖν τῶν ξύλων ὑπέδειξε, κώπην μὲν ναύταις, γεωργοῖς δὲ πτύον, ὁπλίταις δὲ δόρυ παρεχομένη. Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς, πρίν τι τῶν νῦν ὁρωμένων γενέσθαι, εἰς νοῦν βαλόμενος καὶ ὁρμήσας ἀγαγεῖν εἰς γένεσιν τὰ μὴ ὄντα, ὁμοῦ τε ἐνόησεν ὁποῖόν τινα χρὴ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι, καὶ τῷ εἴδει αὐτοῦ τὴν ἁρμόζουσαν ὕλην συναπεγέννησε. Καὶ οὐρανῷ μὲν ἀφώρισε τὴν οὐρανῷ πρέπουσαν φύσιν· τῷ δὲ τῆς γῆς σχήματι τὴν οἰκείαν αὐτῇ καὶ ὀφειλομένην οὐσίαν ὑπέβαλε. Πῦρ δὲ καὶ ὕδωρ καὶ ἀέρα διεσχημάτισέν τε ὡς ἐβούλετο, καὶ εἰς οὐσίαν ἤγαγεν ὡς ὁ ἑκάστου λόγος τῶν γινομένων ἀπῄτει. Ὅλον δὲ τὸν κόσμον ἀνομοιομερῆ τυγχάνοντα ἀρρήκτῳ τινὶ φιλίας θεσμῷ εἰς μίαν κοινωνίαν καὶ ἁρμονίαν συνέ δησεν· ὥστε καὶ τὰ πλεῖστον ἀλλήλων τῇ θέσει διεστηκότα ἡνῶσθαι δοκεῖν διὰ τῆς συμπαθείας. Παυσάσθωσαν οὖν μυθικῶν πλασμάτων, ἐν τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ τῶν οἰκείων λογισμῶν τὴν ἀκατάληπτον διανοίαις καὶ ἄφατον παντελῶς ἀνθρωπίνῃ φωνῇ δύναμιν ἐκμετροῦντες. 2.3 Ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν· οὐκ ἐξ ἡμισείας ἑκάτερον, ἀλλ' ὅλον οὐρανὸν καὶ ὅλην γῆν, αὐτὴν τὴν οὐσίαν τῷ εἴδει συνειλημμένην. Οὐχὶ γὰρ σχημάτων ἐστὶν εὑρέτης, ἀλλ' αὐτῆς τῆς φύσεως τῶν ὄντων δημιουργός. Ἐπεὶ ἀποκρινέσθωσαν ἡμῖν, πῶς ἀλλήλοις συνέτυχον ἥ τε δραστικὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ δύναμις, καὶ ἡ παθητικὴ φύσις τῆς ὕλης· ἡ μὲν τὸ ὑποκείμενον παρεχομένη χωρὶς μορφῆς· ὁ δὲ τῶν σχημάτων τὴν ἐπιστήμην ἔχων, ἄνευ τῆς ὕλης, ἵν' ἑκατέρῳ τὸ ἐνδέον παρὰ θατέρου γένηται· τῷ μὲν δημιουργῷ τὸ ἔχειν ὅπου τὴν τέχνην ἐνεπιδείξηται, τῇ δὲ ὕλῃ τὸ ἀποθέσθαι τὴν ἀμορφίαν καὶ τοῦ εἴδους τὴν στέρησιν. Ἀλλὰ περὶ μὲν τούτων ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον. Πρὸς δὲ τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐπανίωμεν. Ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατα σκεύαστος. Εἰπὼν, Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν· πολλὰ ἀπεσιώπησεν, ὕδωρ, ἀέρα, πῦρ, τὰ ἐκ τούτων ἀπογεννώμενα πάθη· ἃ πάντα μὲν ὡς συμπληρωτικὰ τοῦ κόσμου συνυπέστη τῷ παντὶ δηλονότι· παρέλιπε δὲ ἡ ἱστορία, τὸν ἡμέτερον νοῦν γυμνάζουσα πρὸς ἐντρέχειαν, ἐξ ὀλίγων ἀφορμῶν παρεχομένη ἐπιλογίζεσθαι τὰ λειπόμενα. Ἐπεὶ οὖν οὐκ εἴρηται περὶ τοῦ ὕδατος ὅτι ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς, εἴρηται δὲ ὅτι ἀόρατος ἦν ἡ γῆ· σκόπει σὺ κατὰ σεαυτὸν τίνι παραπετάσματι καλυπτομένη οὐκ ἐξεφαίνετο. Οὔτε οὖν πῦρ αὐτὴν καλύπτειν ἠδύνατο. Φωτιστικὸν γὰρ καὶ καταφάνειαν παρέχον οἷς ἂν προσγένηται μᾶλλον ἢ σκοτῶδες τὸ πῦρ.
thought_title: God creates matter itself, not just form
orientation: Basil is refuting the philosophical idea that matter existed before God and that God only shaped it, arguing instead that God made both the form and the substance of all things.
pass_a_gloss: And from this it follows for them to deny that the great God presided over the constitution of the things that exist, but that, like a contributor to some common feast, he contributed some small portion from himself toward the origin of the things that exist; they were not able, because of the lowliness of their reasonings, to look up to the height of the truth; because here the crafts are later than the materials, having been introduced into life because of the necessity of need. For the wool existed beforehand, and the art of weaving came afterward, filling up from itself what nature lacked. And the wood existed, and carpentry, taking it over, shaping the matter toward the use required on each occasion, showed us the usefulness of wood, providing an oar for sailors, a winnowing fork for farmers, a spear for soldiers. But God, before any of the things now seen came to be, having taken it into his mind and having set out to bring into being the things that were not, at once both thought what sort of thing the world must be, and together with its form he generated the matter suited to it. And for heaven he set apart the nature befitting heaven; and to the shape of the earth he supplied the substance proper to it and owed to it. And fire and water and air he shaped as he willed, and brought into substance as the principle of each of the things coming to be demanded. And the whole world, being of unlike parts, he bound together by some unbreakable bond of friendship into one communion and harmony; so that even the things most distant from one another in position seem to be united through sympathy. Let them cease then from mythical fabrications, measuring by the weakness of their own reasonings the power that is incomprehensible to thought and altogether inexpressible by human speech. God made the heaven and the earth; not each by half, but the whole heaven and the whole earth, the very substance taken together with the form. For he is not a discoverer of shapes, but the maker of the very nature of the things that exist. Since let them answer us, how the active power of God and the passive nature of matter met one another; the one providing the underlying thing without form; and the other having the knowledge of shapes, without the matter, so that to each what was lacking might come from the other; to the maker, the having somewhere to display his craft, and to the matter, the putting off of formlessness and the privation of form. But about these things, so much. Let us return to the beginning. But the earth was invisible and unformed. Having said, In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth, he passed over many things in silence, water, air, fire, the affections generated from these; all of which, as things that fill up the world, clearly came into existence together with the whole; but the narrative omitted them, training our mind toward readiness, providing from few starting points to reason out the things left out. Since therefore it has not been said about the water that God made it, but it has been said that the earth was invisible; consider for yourself by what covering it was hidden and did not appear. Therefore fire could not cover it. For fire is illuminating and provides visibility to whatever it comes upon, rather than being dark.

lemmas.gloss: to look up to, gaze upon

choices.english: a contributor to some common feast
choices.why: ἔρανος is a shared meal to which each brings a portion; Basil's point is that the philosophers reduce God to one contributor among others, not the sole source.
The compound verb stresses that God produced the matter at the same moment as the form, not that matter pre-existed.
This technical term from natural philosophy means composed of dissimilar parts; Basil uses it to emphasize the world's diversity unified by God.

choices.english: by some unbreakable bond of friendship
choices.why: The phrase personifies the cosmic order as a bond of friendship, a common Stoic and Platonic image Basil adopts for divine providence.
rejected: by an indissoluble law of love
by an unbreakable ordinance of affection

choices.why: ἀκατάληπτος is a technical term for what cannot be grasped by the mind; Basil applies it to God's creative power.
Per the glossary, this is the fixed rendering for the initial state of the earth, hidden by water and not yet furnished.

bible_refs.note: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
Ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος

pass_b_english: From this they go on to deny that the great God presided over the constitution of all things, and to claim that he was like a contributor to some common feast, throwing in only a small portion of his own toward the origin of things. They could not, because of the lowliness of their reasoning, look up to the height of the truth: that here among us the crafts come after their materials, since they were introduced into human life by the necessity of need. The wool existed first, and weaving came afterward, supplying from itself what nature lacked. The wood was there, and carpentry took it in hand, shaping the material for whatever need was sought at the time, and showed us the usefulness of wood—providing an oar for sailors, a winnowing fork for farmers, a spear for soldiers. But God, before any of the things now seen came to be, set his mind to it and resolved to bring the things that were not into being; at one and the same moment he thought what kind of world it should be, and generated together with its form the matter that suited it. For heaven he set apart the nature proper to heaven; for the shape of the earth he supplied the substance that belonged to it and was owed to it. Fire and water and air he shaped as he willed, and brought them into being as the principle of each thing that came to be required. And the whole world, being of unlike parts, he bound together by some unbreakable bond of friendship into one communion and harmony, so that even the things most distant from one another in position seem to be united through their mutual sympathy. Let them cease, then, from their mythical fabrications, measuring by the weakness of their own reasoning the power that is incomprehensible to thought and utterly inexpressible by human speech. “God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1)—not each halfway, but the whole heaven and the whole earth, the very substance taken together with the form. For he is not a discoverer of shapes, but the maker of the very nature of things. Otherwise let them answer us: how did the active power of God and the passive nature of matter ever meet one another—the one supplying the underlying thing without form, the other possessing the knowledge of shapes without the matter—so that each might receive from the other what it lacked: the maker having somewhere to display his craft, and the matter putting off its formlessness and its lack of shape? But enough on these matters. Let us return to the beginning. “The earth was invisible and unformed” (Genesis 1:2). When Moses said, “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1), he passed over many things in silence: water, air, fire, and the qualities that arise from them. All of these, as things that complete the world, clearly came into being together with the whole; but the account left them out, training our mind toward quickness, giving us from a few starting points the ability to reason out what remains. Since, then, nothing is said about the water—that God made it—but it is said that the earth was invisible, consider for yourself by what covering it was hidden from view. Fire could not have covered it, for fire gives light and makes visible whatever it comes near, rather than casting darkness.

last_rejected.quote: throwing in only a small portion of his own toward the origin of things
last_rejected.source_quote: ὀλίγην τινὰ μοῖραν εἰς τὴν τῶν ὄντων γένεσιν παρ' ἑαυτοῦ συμβεβλῆσθαι
last_rejected.why: συμβεβλῆσθαι means 'contributed' not 'throwing in'; ἐράνου is a subscription/loan association, not 'common feast'
last_rejected.fix: having contributed only a small portion from himself toward the coming-to-be of things
last_rejected.ruling: συμβεβλῆσθαι = 'throw/contribute in'; ἐράνος = common feast/contribution. English captures the idiom adequately.

last_rejected.quote: supplying from itself what nature lacked
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸ τῆς φύσεως ἐνδέον παρ' ἑαυτῆς ἐκπληροῦσα
last_rejected.why: ἑαυτῆς refers to weaving (feminine), not 'itself' as nature; weaving supplies what nature lacked
last_rejected.fix: supplying from itself what nature lacked
last_rejected.ruling: ἑαυτῆς refers to ὑφαντικὴ (weaving); 'from itself' correctly renders this. No ambiguity or error.

last_rejected.quote: generated together with its form the matter that suited it
last_rejected.source_quote: τῷ εἴδει αὐτοῦ τὴν ἁρμόζουσαν ὕλην συναπεγέννησε
last_rejected.why: συναπεγέννησε means 'generated along with' not 'generated together with its form'; God generated matter together with form
last_rejected.fix: and together with its form generated the matter that suited it
last_rejected.ruling: συναπεγέννησε = 'generated together with'; English 'generated together with its form' captures the sense adequately.

last_rejected.quote: the principle of each thing that came to be required
last_rejected.source_quote: ὡς ὁ ἑκάστου λόγος τῶν γινομένων ἀπῄτει
last_rejected.why: λόγος here means 'rational principle/formula', not 'principle' in a vague sense; it's the logos/reason of each thing
last_rejected.fix: as the rational principle of each thing that came to be demanded
last_rejected.ruling: λόγος rendered 'principle' is within normal range; 'rational principle' is a preference, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: measuring by the weakness of their own reasoning
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐν τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ τῶν οἰκείων λογισμῶν τὴν ἀκατάληπτον διανοίαις καὶ ἄφατον παντελῶς ἀνθρωπίνῃ φωνῇ δύναμιν ἐκμετροῦντες
last_rejected.why: ἐκμετροῦντες takes double accusative: they are 'measuring the power by their weak reasoning', not 'measuring by weakness'
last_rejected.fix: measuring the power that is incomprehensible to thought and utterly inexpressible by human speech by the weakness of their own reasoning
last_rejected.ruling: English 'measuring the power by the weakness' correctly renders ἐκμετροῦντες with double accusative. No error.

last_rejected.quote: the very substance taken together with the form
last_rejected.source_quote: αὐτὴν τὴν οὐσίαν τῷ εἴδει συνειλημμένην
last_rejected.why: συνειλημμένην is passive: 'substance enveloped/taken up together with form', not active 'taken together'
last_rejected.fix: the very substance enveloped together with the form
last_rejected.ruling: συνειλημμένην passive 'taken together with' is correctly rendered; 'enveloped' is a preference, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: the qualities that arise from them
last_rejected.why: πάθη are 'affections/properties' (passive qualities), not 'qualities that arise' as if active; these are the passive states of the elements
last_rejected.ruling: πάθη = 'qualities/affections'; 'qualities that arise from them' captures ἀπογεννώμενα adequately. Minor preference only.

last_rejected.source_quote: τὸν ἡμέτερον νοῦν γυμνάζουσα πρὸς ἐντρέχειαν
last_rejected.why: ἐντρέχεια means 'acuteness/sharpness' of mind, mental agility, not 'quickness' as in speed
last_rejected.ruling: ἐντρέχεια = 'quickness/agility'; 'quickness' is within normal range. Mere preference for 'acuteness'.

last_rejected.quote: giving us from a few starting points the ability to reason out what remains
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐξ ὀλίγων ἀφορμῶν παρεχομένη ἐπιλογίζεσθαι τὰ λειπόμενα
last_rejected.why: ἐπιλογίζεσθαι means 'to infer/conclude by reasoning', not 'reason out'; it's logical inference not working out
last_rejected.fix: giving us from a few starting points the ability to infer what remains
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπιλογίζεσθαι = 'reason out/infer'; both within normal range. 'Reason out' is not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: by what covering it was hidden from view
last_rejected.why: οὐκ ἐξεφαίνετο is imperfect 'was not being revealed/shown forth', not 'hidden from view' as if completed action; ongoing state
last_rejected.fix: by what covering it was not being revealed
last_rejected.ruling: οὐκ ἐξεφαίνετο = 'was not revealed/shown'; 'hidden from view' conveys the same sense adequately. Preference only.

last_rejected.why: σκοτῶδες is adjective 'dark, shadowy'; the phrase means 'fire is more illuminative than dark', not 'rather than casting darkness'
last_rejected.fix: fire being more illuminative than dark
last_rejected.ruling: σκοτῶδες = 'dark'; 'casting darkness' conveys the adjectival sense adequately. Mere preference, not a meaning change.
